original_value: AbstractWe examined student performance in a computer‐supported learning environment after students undertook, among others, a graphing task within an inquiry context. Students were assigned in two conditions: (a) Students were given one variable, and they had to select the second one to construct their graph; (b) students were given four variables, and they had to select two to construct their graph. Both conditions problematized student work by triggering retrospective action, where students returned to previous stages of the learning activity sequence. Retrospective action correlated positively to knowledge gains in Condition 2, where students were more likely to revisit earlier stages of their inquiry. Time‐on‐task, when students passed through learning tasks for the first time, correlated negatively with retrospective action (second pass), which indicated that there was a minimum amount of time needed to effectively execute tasks. Trade‐offs between time‐on‐task (first pass) and retrospective action demarcate a novel field of research.

result.paraphrase: Abstract We examined student performance in a computer-supported learning environment after, among other activities, students completed a graphing task in an inquiry context. Students were assigned to two conditions: (a) one variable was provided and they had to choose the second to create their graph; (b) four variables were provided and they had to choose two to create their graph. In both conditions, student work was problematized by prompting retrospective action, with students returning to earlier stages in the learning activity sequence. Retrospective action was positively associated with knowledge gains in Condition 2, where students were more likely to revisit earlier stages of their inquiry. Time on task during the first pass through learning tasks correlated negatively with retrospective action on the second pass, indicating that a minimum amount of time was needed to carry out tasks effectively. Trade-offs between first-pass time on task and retrospective action define a new research area.
